sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Fleming County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
Fleming County splits the work between the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) and the Fleming County Sheriff, with the County Clerk stepping in once a bill is late. The PVA answers valuation questions at 606-845-1401 and lists weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The sheriff collects at 201 Court Square in Flemingsburg, on the courthouse square, and takes calls at 606-845-4701, option 1, with counter hours of 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday.

The PVA's own description of the job is useful for owners who expect the assessor to lower their bill: it appraises property at fair market value, keeps tax maps and ownership records, handles exemptions and does not set tax rates. Rates come from the fiscal court, the city governments, the school board and other districts. The county's fiscal court meets at the courthouse on the second Tuesday of each month at 9:00 a.m. Eastern.

The PVA or a deputy visits every property at least once every four years, and the law lets the PVA measure the exterior of a building even when nobody is home. If a mailing address changes, tell the PVA in writing so that bills and assessment notices find you.

sections.h2: When are Fleming County property taxes due?
sections.html:
The sheriff follows the state's regular schedule: discount from October 1 to November 1, face amount from November 2 to December 31, then penalties. Bills usually go out near the end of September, and an owner who has not received one must still pay, so call 606-845-4701 and ask for a balance.

The 2026 discount window closed on November 1, 2026, and the face amount applies through December 31. On a $1,000 bill, the early payer saves $20 against the face amount, and a late payer in February owes $1,210.

  • Pay in person, by check made out to the Fleming County Sheriff, by money order, or in cash.
  • Credit cards work in the office or by phone with a 2.5 percent service fee.
  • Mailed payments must be postmarked by the deadline to avoid a penalty.
  • A drop box at the sheriff's entrance is open around the clock and is emptied each morning at 8:00.

sections.h2: How can I appeal a Fleming County property assessment?
sections.html:
You need a PVA conference first, because Kentucky does not let a taxpayer go straight to the board. The tax roll opens for 13 days starting on the first Monday of May. A conference held in that window preserves the right to file with the County Clerk by the end of the workday following the last day of the inspection period.

The Department of Revenue gives an example: if inspection runs May 3 to May 17, the filing deadline is May 18. The local board of assessment appeals then convenes between 25 and 35 days later. Owners should bring documentation, since the board denies an appeal without documentation such as insurance policies, construction costs or sale listings.

  • The PVA must explain how your value was set and write down the outcome of the conference.
  • Anyone paid to represent you must be an attorney, CPA, certified appraiser or licensed broker, among other listed professions, and must carry your written authorization.
  • You may record the board hearing on audio.

The sheriff's office does not hear value disputes and refers them to the PVA. Skipping the hearing after filing ends the right to go to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

sections.h2: Can Fleming County homeowners cut their bill with the homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Yes, if the owner is 65 or older or classified as totally disabled. For the 2025 and 2026 assessment years the state deducts $49,100 from the home's assessed value, then computes tax on the remainder. The county's Census median value is $134,700, so a house at that level would be taxed on $85,600 after the exemption.

The owner files the application with the PVA, supplying a birth certificate, driver's license, passport or other approved proof of age. A disability claim requires a total disability classification from a federal agency or a retirement system and payments for the whole assessment period. Most disability claimants renew yearly, with exceptions for veterans with service-connected disabilities and people found totally and permanently disabled by Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement Systems.

Mortgage borrowers should check how escrow works. The sheriff says that when a lender pays from escrow, the lender handles the payment, yet the homeowner stays ultimately responsible for making sure the tax is paid on time.

sections.h2: What happens to Fleming County taxes if I sell my house?
sections.html:
Tax liability follows ownership, and the sheriff invites buyers and sellers to call about proration based on the closing date. KRS 134.015 makes the tax a personal debt of the owner on the assessment date, and a lien on delinquent property survives a sale for up to 11 years under KRS 134.420. In practice, ask the sheriff for a balance before listing and settle the year's bill through the closing agent.

At the close of business on April 15, every unpaid bill passes to the Fleming County Clerk under KRS 134.122. From that moment, the Department of Revenue's guidance says interest accrues at 1 percent per month, the clerk and county attorney add commissions and a lien fee is charged. The county attorney mails a 30-day notice and, if needed, a second notice within 60 days. The clerk's tax sale falls between 90 and 135 days after the transfer.

The state transfer tax on the deed is $0.50 for each $500 of value, charged to the seller. For a $134,700 sale the figure is $135.00, because the 270th $500 block is only partly filled and still counts in full.

Contact the Fleming County Clerk's office in Flemingsburg for a payoff on any bill already transferred, and ask the PVA to update the mailing address on the account once the sale closes.

sections.h2: What is Fleming County, Kentucky, like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Fleming County was formed in 1798 from Mason County and named for Colonel John Fleming. Flemingsburg is the seat, Ewing is the other city and Elizaville is a census-designated place. The county covers 351 square miles, of which 349 are land, and touches Mason, Lewis, Rowan, Bath, Nicholas and Robertson counties. In 1998 the General Assembly named it the Covered Bridge Capital of Kentucky. The courthouse was rebuilt in 1830 and again in 1952.

The Census Bureau counts the county as 100 percent rural in 2020, and its QuickFacts page gives this picture:

  • Population: 15,787 in 2025, up 4.7 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 74.8 percent across 5,859 households.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $134,700.
  • Median gross rent: $715.
  • Median household income: $49,307.
  • Mean travel time to work: 33.1 minutes.
  • Building permits in 2025: 0.

With no new construction permits reported for 2025, nearly all sales involve existing houses, many of them older. A seller carrying back taxes or needing repairs can compare an as-is cash sale against the cost of fixing a house to list it.

faqs.q: When do Fleming County property tax bills go out?
faqs.a: Bills are typically mailed at the end of September. The sheriff's schedule for 2026 opened the 2 percent discount on October 1. Owners who have not received a bill should call 606-845-4701, option 1.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for paying Fleming County taxes late?
faqs.a: A 5 percent penalty applies from January 1 through January 31, and 21 percent from February 1 through April 15. A bill that is still unpaid on April 15 passes to the County Clerk.

faqs.q: Where is the Fleming County Sheriff's tax office?
faqs.a: It is at 201 Court Square in Flemingsburg, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. There is also a 24 hour drop box at the entrance.

faqs.q: Who do I call to dispute my Fleming County assessment?
faqs.a: Call the Fleming County PVA at 606-845-1401. The sheriff cannot change a value, and a PVA conference is required before any appeal reaches the board.

faqs.q: Does the Fleming County homestead exemption apply to all homeowners?
faqs.a: No. It is limited to owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled and live in the home. The deduction is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years.
